newsitem.title: USA: NYS Senate sees no "will" to get a budget approved.
newsitem.headline: NYS Senate sees no "will" to get a budget approved.

text.p: The New York State Senate Majority Leader Monday said he sees no "will" to get a budget approved, explaining that before progress can be made there first must be an agreement on how much revenues it can expect.

Explaining that the Senate's decision last year to approve its own budget, called a one-houser, had not speeded the process, Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, told reporters in Albany: "In my mind, it's not productive for me to try to lead my conference into a one-houser or anywhere until there's a will to get a budget done. And I don't see the will."

He added: "So my attitude is we're going to lean back, see what happens and let time pass, and just do the best that we can, because the one thing I learned is that one-house budgets aren't law of the state, and it didn't help last year."

The Assembly, which is led by Democrats, has taken a one-house approach this year. New York State last year set a national record for late budgets, and having approved a six-week interim budget last week, looks set to miss the April 1 deadline for the 13th time in a row.

A spokesman for the state Division of Budget said that he understood the Assembly planned to approve on Tuesday an agreement to ensure that debt payments are made on time, even if the budget was late. The Senate evidently approved the bill last week, he added.

Bruno, saying Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, was overly optimistic about his revenue estimates, said Gov George Pataki, a Republican, was focussing on a number of issues, which also was slowing the process.

"The Governor's attitude, I think, is that he has welfare to deal with, criminal justice reform, keeping a lid on spending, rent deregulation, and all of those things are inhibitions to having a budget in place by April 1."

Bruno, who wants to eliminate apartment rent controls, which mainly affect New York City, said there was was no possibility that New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani's suggestion--that the city set its own rules--would be approved by the state Senate. The rules mainly affect New York City residents.

While the June 15 expiry of the rent control rules was expected to be used to pressure the Assembly Speaker, who represents a Manhattan district, Bruno said he did not want to see Pataki use scare tactics. "They don't work," he said.
